{{Expert needed|Mathematics|date=September 2025}}
In the theory of [[orthogonal polynomials]], '''Bochner's theorem''' is a [[Characterization (mathematics)|characterization theorem]] of certain families of orthogonal polynomials as polynomial solutions to [[Sturm–Liouville theory|Sturm–Liouville problems]] with polynomial coefficients.

The theorem is named after [[Salomon Bochner]], who discovered it in 1929.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Bochner |first=S. |date=December 1929 |title=Über Sturm-Liouvillesche Polynomsysteme |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01180560 |journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift |language=de |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=730–736 |doi=10.1007/BF01180560 |issn=0025-5874|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Setup ==
Define notations

* <math>D_x</math> is the [[differential operator]].
* <math>T_1, T_2, \dots</math> are [[Linear map|linear operators]] on functions. For example, <math>g(x) \mapsto f(x) D_x g(x)</math> is one. They are often assumed to be polynomials in <math>x, D_x</math>.
* <math>f_1, f_2, \dots</math> are real or complex functions, and are often assumed to be polynomials.
* <math>\lambda_i</math> are real or complex numbers. They are eigenvalues of linear operators.
* <math>a, b, \alpha, \beta</math> are real or complex numbers. They parameterize the solution families.

A Sturm–Liouville problem is specified as follows: Given functions <math>f_2, f_1, f_0</math> and operators <math>T_2, T_1</math>, solve for <math>\lambda_n, 
y_n</math> in<math display="block">[f_2 T_2 + f_1 T_1 + f_0] y_n = \lambda_n y_n</math>Equivalently, it is solving for the eigenpairs of the operator <math>f_2 T_2 + f_1 T_1 + f_0</math>.

== Statement ==

Let <math>T_2 = D_x^2, T_1 = D_x</math>. Bochner's problem asks the following: consider the SL problem<math display="block">[f_2 D_x^2 + f_1 D_x + f_0] y_n = \lambda_n y_n</math>For what values of <math>f_0, f_1, f_2</math>, are the eigenpairs <math>(\lambda_0, y_0), (\lambda_1, y_1), \dots</math> such that <math>y_0</math> is a polynomial of degree 0, <math>y_1</math> is a polynomial of degree 1, etc? 

Observe first that by plugging in the <math>y_0 = 1</math> solution, we have <math>f_0(x) = \lambda_0</math>, so we may [[Without loss of generality|WLOG]] assume that <math>\lambda_0 = 0, f_0 = 0</math>. Similarly, by plugging in the <math>y_1 = x + a, \; y_2 = x^2 + ax + b</math>, we find that <math>f_1, f_2</math> must be polynomials of degree at most 1, 2 respectively. 

Bochner's theorem states that, up to a complex-affine transform of <math>x</math> (that is, of form <math>x \mapsto ax + b</math>), there are only 5 families of solutions:<ref name=":1">{{cite journal |last1=Kwon |first1=Kil-H. |last2=Littlejohn |first2=Lance L. |date=1997 |title=Classification of classical orthogonal polynomials |url=https://koreascience.kr/article/JAKO199711919485937.page |journal=Journal of the Korean Mathematical Society |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=973–1008}}</ref> 

{| class="wikitable"
|+ 5 polynomial families
! Polynomial solution <math>y_n(x)</math>
! <math>f_2(x)</math>
! <math>f_1(x)</math>
! <math>\lambda_n</math>
!Condition
|-
| [[Jacobi polynomials]] <math>P_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}(x)</math>
| <math>1-x^2</math>
| <math>\beta-\alpha-x(\alpha+\beta+2)</math>
| <math>-n(n+\alpha+\beta+1)</math>
|<math>\alpha, \beta, \alpha+\beta + 1 \not\in\{-1, -2, \dots\}</math>
|-
| [[Laguerre polynomials]] <math>L_n^{(\alpha)}(x)</math>
| <math>x</math>
| <math>1+\alpha-x</math>
| <math>-n</math>
|<math>\alpha \not\in\{-1, -2, \dots\}</math>
|-
| [[Hermite polynomials]] <math>H_n(x)</math>
| <math>1</math>
| <math>-2x</math>
| <math>-2n</math>
|
|-
| [[Bessel polynomials]] <math>y_n(x; a, 1)</math>
| <math>x^2</math>
| <math>ax+1</math>
| <math>n(n+a-1)</math>
|<math>a \not\in\{0, -1, -2, \dots\}</math>
|-
| Monomials <math>x^n</math>
| <math>x^2</math>
| <math>x</math>
| <math>n^2</math>
|
|}

Proof sketch: By the previous observation, there are only 5 parameters in total that characterize the problem:<math display="block">(ax^2 + bx + c)y'' + (dx + e) y' = \lambda y</math>Setting <math>a = 1</math>, then up to a complex affine transform, it reduces to the form<math display="block">(1-x^2)y'' + (dx + e) y' = \lambda y</math>This is the form of the [[Jacobi polynomials#Differential equation|Jacobi differential equation]], and has polynomial solutions precisely when there exists <math>\alpha, \beta</math> such that <math>dx + e = \beta-\alpha-x(\alpha+\beta+2)</math>. These are the Jacobi polynomials. The other cases are, up to affine scaling, the various limits of the <math>a = 1</math> case. The solution families are then obtained by taking the respective limits of the Jacobi polynomials. The conditions on the parameters are necessary to prevent the [[leading coefficient]] from going zero.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Ismail |first=Mourad E. H. |date=2003-10-15 |title=A generalization of a theorem of Bochner |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0377042703005363 |journal=Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics |volume=159 |issue=2 |pages=319–324 |doi=10.1016/S0377-0427(03)00536-3 |issn=0377-0427|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The original proof by Bochner directly considered the 3 possible cases:

* <math>a = 1</math>
* <math>a = 0, b = 1</math>
* <math>a = b = 0, c = 1</math>

and for each, performed a complex-affine transform of the variable and solved the corresponding equation.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

== Extensions ==
The Bochner's theorem allows many extensions, by relaxing various conditions on the setup of Bochner's problem. Other extensions are reviewed in <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Everitt |first1=W. N. |last2=Kwon |first2=K. H. |last3=Littlejohn |first3=L. L. |last4=Wellman |first4=R. |date=2001-08-01 |title=Orthogonal polynomial solutions of linear ordinary differential equations |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0377042700006361 |journal=Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics |series=5th Int. Symp. on Orthogonal Polynomials, Special Functions and t heir Applications |volume=133 |issue=1 |pages=85–109 |doi=10.1016/S0377-0427(00)00636-1 |bibcode=2001JCoAM.133...85E |issn=0377-0427|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and.<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Everitt |first1=W. N. |last2=Littlejohn |first2=L. L. |date=1991 |title=Orthogonal polynomials and spectral theory: a survey |series=IMACS Annals on Computing and Applied Mathematics |volume=9 |pages=21–55 |book-title=Orthogonal polynomials and their applications}}</ref>

=== Real case ===
If instead of complex-affine transforms, we only permit real-affine transforms, then there are 2 more families: twisted Hermite, and twisted Jacobi:<ref name=":1" />
{| class="wikitable"
|+ 2 extra polynomial families
! Polynomial solution <math>y_n(x)</math>
! <math>f_2(x)</math>
! <math>f_1(x)</math>
! <math>\lambda_n</math>
!Condition
|-
| twisted Jacobi polynomials <math>\check{P}_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}(x)</math>
| <math>1+x^2</math>
| <math>i(\beta-\alpha)-x(\alpha+\beta+2)</math>
| <math>n(n+\alpha+\beta+1)</math>
|<math>\alpha+\beta + 1 \not\in\{-1, -2, \dots\}</math>
|-
| twisted Hermite polynomials <math>\check{H}_n(x)</math>
| <math>1</math>
| <math>2x</math>
| <math>2n</math>
|
|}
The 2 extra cases are orthogonal, but not positive-definite. The twisted Hermite satisfies the following complex-orthogonality:<math display="block">\int_{-i \infty}^{i \infty} \check{H}_m(x) \check{H}_n(x) \exp \left(x^2\right) d x=(-1)^n \sqrt{\pi} n!2^{-n} i \delta_{m n} \quad(m \text { and } n \geq 0)</math>They are orthogonal (but not positive-definite) with respect to the real weight function<math display="block">w(x)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { if } x \leq 0 \\ e^{x^2} \int_0^x e^{-t^2} g(t) d t & \text { if } x>0\end{cases}</math>where <math>g</math> is any real function supported on <math>[0, \infty)</math>, that satisfies <math>\int_0^{\infty} e^{-x^2} g(x) d x=0</math>, and has all [[Moment (mathematics)|moments]] zero.

The twisted Jacobi satisfies the following complex-orthogonality:<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
&\begin{aligned}
& \left\langle(1-x)_{+}^\alpha(1+x)_{+}^\beta, \check{P}_m^{(\alpha, \beta)}(i x) \check{P}_n^{(\alpha, \beta)}(i x)\right\rangle \\
& =\frac{(-1)^n 2^{2 n+\alpha+\beta+1} \Gamma(n+\alpha+1) \Gamma(n+\beta+1) \Gamma(n+\alpha+\beta+1) n!}{\Gamma(2 n+\alpha+\beta+1) \Gamma(2 n+\alpha+\beta+2)} \delta_{m n}
\end{aligned}\\
&(m \text { and } n \geq 0)
\end{aligned}</math>where the average is taken over the function <math>\left(1+x^2\right)^{\frac{2-d}{2}} e^{i(\beta - \alpha) \arctan x}</math>.

They are orthogonal (but not positive-definite) with respect to the real weight function<math display="block">w(x)=e^{f(x)}\left[c+\int_0^x e^{-f(t)}\left(1+t^2\right)^{-1} g(t) d t\right]</math>where <math>g</math> is any real function supported on <math>[0, \infty)</math>, that satisfies <math>\int_0^{\infty} e^{-f(t)}\left(1+t^2\right)^{-1} g(t) d t=0</math>, and has all moments zero.

=== Exceptional ===
The original Bochner's theorem assumes that there exists one polynomial solution per degree. If we relax this assumption, then we obtain the '''exceptional''' polynomial families. In an exception polynomial family, some degrees may not correspond to any polynomial. Such a family does not make up a complete basis for the function space, because certain polynomial functions cannot be expressed as a linear combination of its elements, but such a family may still have certain applications.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gómez-Ullate |first1=David |last2=Kamran |first2=Niky |last3=Milson |first3=Robert |date=2010-05-01 |title=An extension of Bochner's problem: Exceptional invariant subspaces |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0021904509001853 |journal=Journal of Approximation Theory |volume=162 |issue=5 |pages=987–1006 |doi=10.1016/j.jat.2009.11.002 |issn=0021-9045|arxiv=0805.3376 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gómez-Ullate |first1=David |last2=Kamran |first2=Niky |last3=Milson |first3=Robert |date=2009-11-01 |title=An extended class of orthogonal polynomials defined by a Sturm–Liouville problem |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022247X09004569 |journal=Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications |volume=359 |issue=1 |pages=352–367 |doi=10.1016/j.jmaa.2009.05.052 |issn=0022-247X|arxiv=0807.3939 }}</ref>
